failing_part: "it raises the AUC and corrects the model's tendency to underestimate the rarer class's probability, so the decision threshold can stay at 0.5"
narrowest_regime: None for risk prediction. Resampling only shifts the intercept toward 50% prevalence; it can mimic a cost-weighted classifier at 0.5 when only hard labels are wanted and calibrated probabilities are not, but the cited paper's conclusion is the opposite of this default.
reason: The cited paper (van den Goorbergh et al., JAMIA 2022) found that random oversampling, undersampling and SMOTE did not raise AUC compared with no correction, and that they strongly overestimated the minority-class probability. Its conclusion was that 'imbalance correction may even worsen model performance'. Maximum-likelihood logistic regression is already calibrated in the large on its training data, apart from a small rare-events bias in small samples. Resampling to balance replaces that small bias with a large upward bias, so a 0.5 threshold on resampled-model probabilities is not a corrected threshold; it is a hidden change of misclassification costs.

citations.cite: van den Goorbergh R, van Smeden M, Timmerman D, Van Calster B. The harm of class imbalance corrections for risk prediction models: illustration and simulation using logistic regression. JAMIA 2022;29(9):1525-1534
King G, Zeng L. Logistic regression in rare events data. Political Analysis 2001;9:137-163

bite_note: As a default, it would miscalibrate every rare-outcome risk model the app fits (predicted risks inflated, often several-fold) and set a 0.5 threshold that classifies far too many rows as positive. The natural alternative is no resampling, with a threshold chosen from the costs or a decision curve.

failing_part: "ordinary unweighted K-fold cross-validation with folds drawn at random over rows estimates the surveyed population's performance without bias, because randomly drawn folds are themselves simple random samples of the design"
narrowest_regime: Only when the weights are uninformative for the loss (equal-probability selection, or the loss unrelated to the selection probabilities) and outcomes are uncorrelated within PSUs. In that case the survey is effectively a simple random sample.
reason: Folds drawn at random over rows are simple random samples of the sample, not of the population. Unweighted CV therefore estimates the expected loss under the sample's (unequal-probability) distribution. The population loss is the weight-weighted loss, E_s[wL]/E_s[w], and the two differ whenever selection probability is related to the error. In a simulation with an oversampled stratum, unweighted CV gave a mean MSE of 2.34, while weighted CV gave 3.68 against a true population MSE of 3.67. Wieczorek, Guerin & McMahon (2022), the paper the claim cites, recommend the opposite: keep each PSU within one fold, include every stratum in each fold, and weight the test errors.

citations.cite: Wieczorek J, Guerin C, McMahon T. K-fold cross-validation for complex sample surveys. Stat 2022;11:e454 (doi:10.1002/sta4.454); design-based folds and weighted test error, per the abstract and the authors' surveyCV package documentation

bite_note: Population performance is misestimated, by about 36% too low (optimistic) in the simulated stratified design. Splitting PSUs across folds adds further optimism, and model or tuning choices made on the wrong error can flip. The natural alternative is design-based folds with weighted test error.

narrowest_regime: OLS with classical, heteroskedasticity-robust (HC0-HC3) or cluster-robust intervals, in exact arithmetic; floating-point differences are about 1e-15. The exception is order-dependent interval methods: HAC/Newey-West intervals, block bootstraps, and a seeded bootstrap, whose resamples change with row order (Monte Carlo noise only). For HAC, sorting rows changed the SEs by up to 16% in a check. There, not shuffling is correct anyway.
reason: X'X = sum_i x_i x_i' and X'y = sum_i x_i y_i are sums over rows, so a permutation leaves beta-hat, the residual sum of squares and every per-row fitted value unchanged. Classical, HC and cluster sandwich variances are also sums over rows or clusters, so the intervals are unchanged too. A numerical check gave coefficient, SE and fitted-value differences of about 1e-15. The default of not shuffling follows, and it is also the right choice for order-dependent methods like HAC.
bite_note: Shuffling or not gives identical OLS results, so the default changes nothing for the fit. It matters only for downstream order-dependent steps (unshuffled K-fold assignment, HAC), and for those not shuffling is the safe choice.

failing_part: "only flips the sign of that column's own coefficient, so the finding's repair changes no reported number" ... "any outcome type or model family the primary uses"
narrowest_regime: Models whose design contains the constant: an intercept, fixed effects, strata, or the Cox baseline hazard. The fit must be unpenalized ML/OLS/GLM/Cox/quantile regression, or penalized with an unpenalized intercept and a sign-symmetric penalty, and the relabeled column must enter no interaction. There the exposure coefficient, its SE and the fitted values are invariant. Even there, the intercept is not.
reason: Recoding x to 1-x is an invertible linear reparameterization that preserves the column space whenever the constant is in the design, so fitted values and the exposure's coefficient and interval are unchanged. A check confirmed this to about 1e-16 for logistic and Cox models. But the intercept shifts by the column's coefficient (-0.495 to 0.435 in the check), so it is not true that only the column's own sign flips. If the column enters any covariate-covariate interaction, the other covariate's main effect changes (0.127 to 0.390). With a penalized intercept (liblinear) or a Bayesian prior on a non-centered intercept, even the exposure coefficient moves (0.4852 to 0.4876). FWL gives column-space invariance; it does not make the claim hold for 'any model family'.

citations.cite: Frisch R, Waugh FV. Partial time regressions as compared with individual trends. Econometrica 1933;1:387-401; Lovell MC. Seasonal adjustment of economic time series. JASA 1963;58:993-1010 (column-space/partialling invariance)

bite_note: For the exposure finding, closing it without calibration changes nothing, because the exposure estimate and interval are invariant in the realistic models. It would bite only if a reported intercept, a baseline mean under Describe, or a covariate main effect in an interaction were presented as unchanged.

failing_part: "are pre-exposure common causes of the exposure and the outcome" ... "after exposure no" ... "any study design, including cross-sectional"
narrowest_regime: Fixed-at-birth or early-fixed demographics (age, sex, race/ethnicity as a proxy for unmeasured social causes, and usually completed education in adults), measured or known to precede the exposure. There, VanderWeele's criterion does put them in the adjustment set. It holds less firmly for income/poverty ratio, occupation and marital status, which can be consequences of the exposure or the outcome.
reason: VanderWeele's modified disjunctive cause criterion adjusts for any covariate that causes the exposure OR the outcome. It needs no common-cause answer, excludes instruments, and admits proxies, so pre-filling 'yes/yes' asserts more than the criterion uses. More materially, VanderWeele warns that when the exposure and covariates are measured at the same time, a covariate may be affected by the exposure. Income, occupation and marital status can be downstream of a dietary or alcohol exposure, or of the outcome itself (for example obesity, depression or CVD reducing employment). In cross-sectional data, 'after exposure: no' is an assumption, not a fact, and adjusting for a descendant of the exposure or outcome can bias the total effect.

citations.cite: VanderWeele TJ. Principles of confounder selection. Eur J Epidemiol 2019;34(3):211-219 (modified disjunctive cause criterion; caution on simultaneously measured covariates)

bite_note: Answers confirmed with one tap set the adjustment set. For SES-type covariates in cross-sectional nutrition data, this can adjust away part of a total effect (mediator) or open a collider path, where the natural alternative would be to leave them out or put them in a sensitivity model.

narrowest_regime: As stated. The non-collapsibility part applies to OR and HR with a common outcome, or a high cumulative incidence for HR, and the change is negligible for rare outcomes. Blocking for other estimands rests on the weaker reason that CIE contributes no structural information, together with post-selection inference concerns.
reason: A change in estimate occurs whenever adding a covariate alters the coefficient, which is true of confounders, mediators and colliders alike. The criterion therefore cannot tell them apart; VanderWeele (2019) notes that 'statistical analyses cannot in general distinguish between confounders ... versus mediators'. For a non-collapsible measure (OR, or HR with common events), adding a pure outcome predictor changes the conditional estimate even in a randomized trial. VanderWeele calls change-in-estimate 'inappropriate for non-collapsible measures such as the odds ratio or hazard ratio if the outcome is common'. Both premises hold, and refusing CIE under inference is a defensible consequence.

citations.cite: VanderWeele TJ. Principles of confounder selection. Eur J Epidemiol 2019;34:211-219
Greenland S, Robins JM, Pearl J. Confounding and collapsibility in causal inference. Statistical Science 1999;14:29-46

bite_note: Refusing CIE keeps covariates that a 10% rule would drop or add. With a logistic/Cox model and a common outcome, a CIE-driven set would select prognostic covariates on non-collapsibility shifts rather than confounding.

failing_part: "(e.g., no 24-hour recall for a clinic use)"; also "only predictors recorded at that moment" (the test is 'available at', not 'recorded at')
narrowest_regime: The principle holds as PROBAST 2.3 states it: exclude predictors that are not available when the model is intended to be used. That includes information that only becomes known later (a second recall day, later labs, post-baseline treatment). Whether a 24-hour recall qualifies depends on the intended setting's workflow, not on its being a recall.
reason: PROBAST signalling question 2.3 ('Are all predictors available at the time the model is intended to be used?') is verified. Using unavailable or later-known predictors makes reported performance unattainable in use, and may leak outcome information. A 24-hour recall, however, describes the previous day and is collected at the encounter. It is a standard part of clinical dietetic assessment, and in NHANES the day-1 recall is taken at the MEC exam itself; only the day-2 recall comes later. So the blanket example misapplies the principle: it treats 'not routinely collected in some clinics' as 'known only after the moment of use'. The direction 'looks better in a paper' is also a tendency that depends on the predictor being informative, not a guarantee.

citations.cite: Wolff RF et al. PROBAST: a tool to assess the risk of bias and applicability of prediction model studies. Ann Intern Med 2019;170:51-58; PROBAST form, signalling question 2.3

bite_note: Applied as a default, the example strips dietary-intake predictors (day-1 recall) from a model intended for a dietetic clinic, where they are available at the visit. The model then loses its key predictors and may be weaker than it needs to be.

failing_part: "rows are dropped only for blanks in the predictors" and "Blanks in a column whose blanks are coded as their own 'Missing' level are values, not missing data" (goal = any)
narrowest_regime: Prediction, where a 'Missing' level is a legitimate predictor if blanks arise the same way at deployment, and where rows with a blank outcome (or blank design/time/event fields) are removed upstream. As a description of which predictor blanks drop rows, the engineering rule is coherent. The deferral of unconfirmed roles is an engineering choice with no methods problem.
reason: A complete-case analysis must also drop rows with a blank outcome, exposure, survey weight/PSU/stratum, offset, or time/event indicator. 'Only predictors' is right only if those are handled elsewhere. Recoding blanks as a 'Missing' level does not make them observed data: it is the missing-indicator (missing-category) method. In non-randomized estimation, Groenwold et al. (2012) show it 'will almost always give biased results', whether the data are MCAR or MAR, because the incomplete rows are only partly adjusted for the confounder. Under Estimate, calling such a column's blanks 'values, not missing data' inside a 'complete cases' answer hides a biased hybrid analysis.

citations.cite: Groenwold RHH, White IR, Donders ART, Carpenter JR, Altman DG, Moons KGM. Missing covariate data in clinical research: when and when not to use the missing-indicator method for analysis. CMAJ 2012;184(11):1265-1269

Vach W, Blettner M. Biased estimation of the odds ratio in case-control studies due to the use of ad hoc methods of correcting for missing values for confounding variables. Am J Epidemiol 1991;134:895-907

bite_note: Under Estimate, a confounder with a 'Missing' level keeps the incomplete rows with only partial adjustment, so the exposure effect is biased compared with true complete cases or multiple imputation. Under Predict there is little or no bite.

narrowest_regime: Classical-error regression calibration with replicate measures, simulated at n = 40-250 and reliability 0.20-0.40. Conditional on the interval being shown (at least 90% of resamples calibrated), coverage was 0.946-0.967. The 90% floor and B = 200 are unsourced conventions. B = 200 is below the B >= 1000 usually advised for percentile endpoints (Efron & Tibshirani), which affects endpoint reproducibility more than coverage: 0.950 at B = 200 against 0.940 at B = 1000 in one cell.
reason: Dropped resamples are those with between-person variance estimated at or below zero, i.e. reliability near zero and an unbounded correction. Dropping them truncates the tail away from zero, exactly as the caveat says. In simulation, conditional on display, the far-end miss rate was 3.3-5.3% against a nominal 2.5%, while the near-end miss rate was about 0%. Overall coverage stayed about nominal (0.95-0.97), so the caveat is accurate and not understated. A stricter all-resamples gate did worse (coverage 0.81-0.88 when shown), because it selects datasets whose reliability was overestimated by chance.

citations.cite: Efron B, Tibshirani RJ. An Introduction to the Bootstrap. Chapman & Hall 1993 (B on the order of 1000 for percentile intervals)
Carroll RJ, Ruppert D, Stefanski LA, Crainiceanu CM. Measurement Error in Nonlinear Models, 2nd ed. 2006 (bootstrap for regression calibration)

bite_note: When the interval is shown it is close to nominal, and the lopsided far-end miss is about 2 percentage points. The gate does withhold the interval in 26-40% of small-n, low-reliability datasets, where showing it anyway with failed resamples dropped would have covered 94-96%. That reporting choice costs some intervals but does not make any shown interval wrong.

failing_part: "at least 10 rows and, for a yes/no outcome, at least 5 rows of each class" (no methods basis); "grouped into thirds at its 1/3 and 2/3 quantiles" (a convention)
narrowest_regime: Scoring with nominal intervals needs considerably more than the floor. In simulation, AUC interval coverage reached about 0.93 only at around 25 per class. Validation sample-size guidance (Riley/Collins) targets on the order of 100+ events for precise calibration. Tertiles of an amount column are a defensible but arbitrary convention.
reason: TRIPOD+AI item 23a (verified) asks for performance with confidence intervals in key subgroups and sets no minimum size. Item 14 concerns fairness approaches. Neither supports 10 rows / 5 per class, and the claim admits the thresholds have no source. At the floor, the intervals are not valid: with 5 events and 5 non-events, nominal 95% AUC intervals covered 0.863 (stratified percentile bootstrap) and 0.866 (DeLong), and a calibration slope could not be fitted (separation) in 12% of subgroups. The rule 'refuse below the floor' is reasonable in form, but the floor itself is unjustified and too low for the intervals it promises.

citations.cite: Collins GS et al. TRIPOD+AI statement. BMJ 2024;385:e078378, items 14 and 23a
Riley RD et al. Minimum sample size for external validation of a clinical prediction model with a binary outcome. Stat Med 2021;40:4230-4251

bite_note: Subgroups at 5-10 per class are scored with intervals that undercover by about 9 percentage points and with unstable calibration. A researcher may infer subgroup underperformance or unfairness from noise, where the natural alternative is a higher floor, or naming the subgroup with 'too few to score'.

narrowest_regime: k >= 3 cycles (t(k-2) is undefined at k = 2 and extremely wide at k = 3). The back-transformed pooled log-MSE estimates the median cycle MSE, which under heterogeneity sits slightly below the mean (by about exp(tau^2/2)). The identity-scale optimism the claim cites is material only at small cycle sizes: about -2.6% at n = 100 per cycle, -0.6% at n = 500, and about 0 at several thousand.
reason: For MSE, SE(MSE_i) is about MSE_i*sqrt(2/n) (for normal errors), so inverse-variance weights on the identity scale fall as MSE rises and the pooled value is pulled low. Simulation confirmed this in every cell (for example 0.974 against a true 1.000 at n = 100, tau = 0). On the log scale, the SE is about sqrt(2/n), independent of level. HKSJ is well supported (IntHout et al. 2014: DL error rates can exceed 30% with few studies). In simulation with 8 cycles, HKSJ covered 0.945-0.957 while DL covered 0.91-0.93 under heterogeneity. The t(k-2) prediction interval is Higgins, Thompson & Spiegelhalter's (2009) recommendation. Snell et al. (2018) did not study MSE, but they support transformed scales for ratio-type measures.

citations.cite: IntHout J, Ioannidis JPA, Borm GF. The Hartung-Knapp-Sidik-Jonkman method for random effects meta-analysis is straightforward and considerably outperforms the standard DerSimonian-Laird method. BMC Med Res Methodol 2014;14:25
Higgins JPT, Thompson SG, Spiegelhalter DJ. A re-evaluation of random-effects meta-analysis. JRSS A 2009;172:137-159 (prediction interval on t with k-2 df)
Riley RD et al. External validation of clinical prediction models using big datasets from e-health records or IPD meta-analysis: opportunities and challenges. BMJ 2016;353:i3140

Snell KIE, Ensor J, Debray TPA, Moons KGM, Riley RD. Meta-analysis of prediction model performance across multiple studies: which scale helps ensure between-study normality for the C-statistic and calibration measures? Stat Methods Med Res 2018;27:3505-3522

bite_note: The bite comes through HKSJ and the prediction interval: against the natural DL alternative, intervals are wider and coverage holds near nominal (DL about 0.91) when cycles are few or heterogeneous. Choosing the log scale over the identity scale changes the pooled MSE negligibly at survey-cycle sizes.

failing_part: "without the optimism of picking the best flexible family" (it replaces the optimism with a pessimistic bias) and "when its 95% percentile interval spans 0 there is 'no measurable cost on these rows'", together with the ">=10 scored rows" floor
narrowest_regime: A primary proper score with moderate-to-large n (hundreds of rows or more), treating the interval as a conservative, roughly 99%, band conditional on the fitted models. There, BBC over the flexible set removes the winner's-curse optimism, at the price of a small pessimistic bias against the flexible pick.
reason: Tsamardinos et al. (verified) evaluate the in-bag winner on out-of-bag rows. They report that BBC-CV is 'somewhat more conservative' (up to 0.034 accuracy at N = 20) and that its percentile CIs are 'mainly conservative', becoming accurate only as n grows. Applied to the paired difference, the procedure tilts toward a smaller cost of interpretability: in simulation the true cost of 0.10 was estimated as 0.074 at n = 30 with 3 flexible families. Its intervals spanned 0 in 98-100% of null cases, and in 57% of cases at n = 100 with a real cost, against about 35% for a correct 95% paired interval. At the stated floor of 10 rows, out-of-bag sets hold about 4 rows. Coverage fell to 0.85-0.88, and a calibration slope cannot be estimated on 4 rows. Rudin (2019) is a normative position and offers no support for the estimator.

citations.cite: Tsamardinos I, Greasidou E, Borboudakis G. Bootstrapping the out-of-sample predictions for efficient and accurate cross-validation. Machine Learning 2018;107:1895-1922 (arXiv:1708.07180)
Rudin C. Stop explaining black box machine learning models for high stakes decisions and use interpretable models instead. Nat Mach Intell 2019;1:206-215

bite_note: The readout says 'no measurable cost' more often than a calibrated 95% interval would, and understates the cost at small n. That nudges researchers toward the interpretable model, and at the 10-row floor the calibration comparison is unestimable.
